doc.title: Marty Napoleon interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York, New York, January 16, 1999

title: Teddy Powell's band, Charlie Ventura and Marty's brother Teddy
summary: Marty recounts Teddy Powell's band, Ventura leaving for Krupa, recommending his brother, and quitting Powell.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: My goodness. And then you went on to Lee Castle and Charlie Barnet.
Charlie Barnet. That was a story, Charlie Barnet’s band. I was reading Down Beat magazine. You got your own list —
I’ve got my own list here.
Do you know about all these things? Oh you must have gotten it from what?

Grove Dictionary, right okay. Anyway so the Charlie Barnet thing was like I was sitting at home, I had just left Teddy Powell’s band or Lee Castle’s band. Teddy Powell’s band I think. That’s another story, that Teddy Powell was weird. Because in Teddy Powell’s band, we had Charlie Ventura on the band, it was magnificent. And Teddy loved him and he used to have arrangements written for Charlie that Charlie would play. He would feature him, and he’d play the introduction [scats] and when he got a call from Gene Krupa was starting another band, so he called Charlie and he says, “Charlie I’m starting a symphonic orchestra,” he says, “you got it.” So he gave his notice to Teddy. In fact Charlie says to me, “I got a call from Gene and he needs a piano player and I told him

about you, I says, “see if he wants to come with the band.” And I said, “oh I’d love to but my brother Teddy’s in New York, I don’t think he’s working and I’ve got a job.” So he says, “you would do that for your brother?” I said, “hey he’s my brother man. I’ve got a job with Teddy Powell, so call my brother.” And he called my brother and he was available and he took the job, he went with Gene. So now Teddy takes the job with Gene and I’m with Powell’s band, oh then when Charlie gave his notice, we’re doing a date in a ballroom someplace in Milwaukee or someplace, no it doesn’t matter, St. Louis, Missouri, I remember everything, and Charlie’s doing his solo up front, and Teddy used to walk back and forth while he was playing his solo, and some kid says, “hey Teddy, man, he’s fantastic.” And I’m listening to him, he’s standing by the piano see. So he says, “you think he’s great, wait until you hear the guy I’ve got coming in, Teddy Nash.” First he’s great, then he’s not that good because he gave his notice. So that’s the kind of guy he was. So now I gave my notice, because he was getting on my nerves for some reason I forget. So I look at my itinerary. I gave a two week notice, and on the 14th day of my notice, no the 13th day of my notice we have a day off in New York City, and the 14th day of my notice is in Toronto, Canada. Now when you give your notice to a band on the road, and you quit, you have to pay your way home. If he fires you he pays your transportation home. So I went to him and I said, “hey Teddy, you know I notice on the 13th day we have a day off in New York City, why don’t you get a piano player to start in Toronto.” He says, “oh no, you gave a two week notice and your date is—” So I said, I’ve got to get away from this band. So I quit the band. So anyway one little thing about Teddy Powell and Chico Marx was that Chico Marx was a fantastic man. He wouldn’t go to dinner alone, he would always take a group of guys from the band with him. He loved to eat with a group of people. And he always paid for everything. I saved a lot of money that way you know. So when I went with Teddy Powell’s band, the first night on the job after the job the guys went to get some hamburgers and things, and when the waitress came with the check he says, “I’ll take it.” So he took the check and he says, “you owe me sixty cents.” I said, “hey Teddy, that ain’t the way it’s supposed to go.
That’s not what I’m used to.
